title: 35. Use of paddy rice in feedlot-finished steers: effect of grain moisture level and processing method on animal performance.
content:
Abstract
The use of rough rice grain, also known as paddy rice, in cattle feeding is not a frequent practice; however, under certain market conditions, it could represent an interesting alternative to improve rice grain value. Because the primary destination of this grain is human consumption, the available information on its use in beef cattle feeding is relatively scarce. This work aimed to evaluate the effect of partial replacement of ground dry corn grain (C) with rough rice (R), differing in processing method (ground, G, vs. cracked, C) and moisture level (9 vs. 20%), on the performance of feedlot-finished steers. Forty-eight Hereford steers (364 ± 18 kg) were used in a 78-d feedlot trial. Animals were blocked by initial BW and randomly assigned to one of four treatments. Steers were distributed into 16 outdoor pens (3 animals/pen and 4 pens/treatment) equipped with feeders and water troughs, with ad libitum access to water. Four TMR (Table 1) with a constant forage-to-concentrate ratio (20:80) were evaluated. Treatments were diets containing 45% of: 1) ground dry C (CG9%), 2) ground dry R (RG9%), 3) cracked dry R (RC9%), or 4) cracked high-moisture R (RC20%). Diets were offered ad libitum in two equal daily meals at 08:30 and 14:30 h. BW was registered every 14 days. Feed offered and refusals were measured daily to determine DMI. Feed-to-Gain ratio (F:G) was calculated using DMI and ADG. All steers were slaughtered on a fixed date at a commercial abattoir. Data was analyzed using a randomized block design, considering the pen as the experimental unit. Treatments were compared using orthogonal contrasts, designed to quantify the effect of grain type (CG9% vs. RG9%), R processing method (RG9% vs. RC9%), and R moisture level (RC9% vs. RC20%). Results indicate (Table 2) that, under the same processing method and moisture level, partial replacement of C with R did not affect ADG, DMI or F:G (p > 0.05). At the same moisture level, no differences were found in ADG or DMI (p > 0.05) between animals receiving ground or cracked R; however, RG9% resulted in a 7% improvement in F:G compared with RC9% (6.75 vs. 7.23 kg DM/kg BW, p < 0.05). Within cracked R diets, increasing grain moisture from 9% to 20% enhanced F:G, resulting in an 8% improvement compared with dry R (6.69 vs. 7.23 kg DM/kg BW; p < 0.05). These results highlight the potential of R as an alternative feed ingredient for feedlot cattle. Management variables such as processing method and moisture content were key to enhancing the nutritional value of R.
